title: How Google Trends Normalization Works
what_it_is: Google Trends normalizes all search volume to 0–100 relative to the PEAK in your chosen time window and geography. It does not show absolute search counts.
why_it_matters: A score of 100 for an obscure name like 'Jennifer Faumuina' might represent a single search in a region of millions of people. That same 100 means something very different if it's for 'Taylor Swift' or 'Donald Trump.'
low_volume_problem: For niche terms (names, local references, compound queries), noise and data artifacts dominate the signal. One person searching, one bot scanning, one typo correction — all render as 100.

scenarios.name: High-volume term (e.g., 'Charlie Kirk')
scenarios.description: Millions of searches across a time window. Spikes are real movements in aggregate interest.
scenarios.example_interpretation: A spike to 100 reflects genuine increase in search activity among large population.
scenarios.reliability: Higher — noise is diluted by volume.

scenarios.name: Medium-volume name (e.g., 'Tyler Robinson' or 'Lance Twiggs')
scenarios.description: Hundreds or low thousands of searches. Spikes can reflect news cycles, trial dates, media coverage.
scenarios.example_interpretation: A spike might reflect news coverage or a hearing, but also might be search-engine bots, data artifacts, or regional population fluctuations.
scenarios.reliability: Moderate — requires context and control groups.

scenarios.name: Low-volume name (e.g., 'Jennifer Faumuina', 'Shaner Broderick', 'Rick Cutler')
scenarios.description: Tens or low hundreds of searches total in a large region. A single search renders as 100 if it's the peak.
scenarios.example_interpretation: A score of 100 for 'Jennifer Faumuina' in 'Israel' likely represents one person, one bot, one misclick. Treat as hypothesis, not signal.

control_group_principle: Test matched names the same way as your targets. If targets are uniquely spiking and controls are clean, you have a signal. If controls also spike identically, the method itself is unreliable for the data you're working with.
why_controls_matter_here: In this dataset, matched controls (Justin Davis, Chris Bagley, Brian Davis, Jennifer Faumuina, etc.) were searched the same way in the same regions. Result: 'No convincing anomaly found' on every one. That means either: (1) the method is too noisy for names this obscure, or (2) the spikes in the main dataset are data artifacts, not foreknowledge signals. The control result suggests (1) and (2).

this_dataset.interpretation: Zero primary Google exports. 89% of records come from two secondary sources (one Threadreader thread, one screenshot compilation), with all records tagged 'Israel' and drawn from names that are mostly low-volume. Without control group testing, this looks like a pattern. With it, the pattern disappears.
